extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in number theory (including graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain the structure, key ingredients, and verification steps of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem (the proof of the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves and the consequent proof of FLT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove modularity for semistable elliptic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles proved the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves, from which Fermat’s Last Theorem follows using proof by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The route to FLT is to show all semistable elliptic curves are modular; combined with Ribet's theorem (which shows a Frey curve from a counterexample would be non-modular) this gives the contradiction that proves FLT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction linking Frey curve and modularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by assuming Fermat's Last Theorem is false, construct a Frey curve from a hypothetical solution, and use Ribet's theorem to show that curve would be non-modular; then prove such curves must be modular to obtain a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explicitly frames the overall strategy as: assume a counterexample exists → Frey curve is non-modular (Ribet) → prove all semistable curves are modular (Wiles) → contradiction, so FLT is true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ribet's theorem (epsilon conjecture) as a necessary link
rubrics_metrics.description: Ribet's theorem shows that the Frey curve associated to a hypothetical solution to Fermat's equation cannot be modular, establishing the link between a counterexample to Fermat and non-modularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes Ribet's proof of Serre's epsilon conjecture as the step that connects hypothetical Fermat counterexamples to the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture, so any complete proof must use this link or an equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct the Frey curve from hypothetical integer solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate a hypothetical solution (a,b,c,n) of Fermat's equation with the elliptic (Frey) curve y^2 = x(x-a^n)(x+b^n) and study its special properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Frey curve must be shown to have the specific properties (arising from high powers) that make Ribet's theorem applicable; the construction is central to the contradiction argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a modularity lifting theorem (Raising modularity from representations to curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that if the geometric Galois representation ρ(E,p) of a semistable elliptic curve E is irreducible and modular (for some prime p>2), then, subject to technical conditions, E itself is modular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'lifting theorem' is the central technical accomplishment: it lets one deduce modularity of curves from modularity of a single Galois representation; it also implies proving modularity for one prime p>2 suffices for a curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove Galois representations of all semistable elliptic curves are modular
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that the geometric Galois representations ρ(E,p) for semistable elliptic curves are modular (for appropriate primes), so that the lifting theorem applies and yields modularity of the curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles's program reduces the problem to proving modularity of representations and then uses the lifting theorem to pass to curves; completeness over all semistable curves (handling every relevant representation) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle reducible and irreducible cases separately (case analysis completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize semistable elliptic curves based on reducibility of their Galois representations and treat each case (irreducible vs reducible) with appropriate methods (including switching primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof splits depending on whether ρ(E,3) is reducible or irreducible; completeness requires covering all possible cases and showing modularity in each.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3–5 switch technique (use of p=3 and p=5 strategically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use p=3 where ρ(E,3) is irreducible (applying Langlands–Tunnell) and p=5 in the reducible situations, employing a 3–5 switch to ensure every case yields modularity for some prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that choosing p=3 is convenient when representations are irreducible (Langlands–Tunnell applies), while p=5 is used in other cases; the 3–5 trick is essential to cover difficult cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established external results (Langlands–Tunnell and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on prior theorems such as Langlands–Tunnell (mod 3 representations are modular) and previously proven parts of the modularity conjecture as building blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof depends on known results for certain primes/representations; a valid proof must correctly incorporate and apply these theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish R = T isomorphism via a numerical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Define deformation rings R and Hecke rings T and show the natural homomorphism R → T is an isomorphism (R = T); Wiles observed this holds iff two abelian groups are finite and have the same cardinality (the 'numerical criterion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the proof is devoted to verifying the hypotheses that make R → T an isomorphism (complete intersection/Gorenstein properties, congruences between Hecke rings, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a class number formula (CNF) and counting/lifting argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a class number formula (CNF) and use induction/counting arguments comparing lifts of mod ℓ^n Galois representations and lifts of modular forms to show existence of a single modular form matching all lifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles attempted a CNF via horizontal Iwasawa theory, later used Euler systems (Kolyvagin–Flach) to build the CNF; the inductive counting argument requires precise control of lifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose sufficient conditions on Galois representations to control lifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a sufficient set of local/global conditions on Galois representations so that the number of lifts is controlled (otherwise too many non-modular lifts exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that without these conditions there will be too many lifts; the conditions must be satisfied by representations coming both from modular forms and from elliptic curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete technical treatment of deformation cases (including flat case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the treatment of deformations, identify and handle the four deformation cases (with the flat deformation case requiring extra work and treated separately in the companion paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles divided the technical proof into cases and used a second paper (with Taylor) to treat technical ring-theoretic issues; a full proof must address all deformation cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure rigorous peer review, vetting, and correction of gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject manuscripts to careful referee review and collaborate to correct any errors found; Wiles's original submission contained an error discovered during review and was corrected in collaboration with Richard Taylor before final publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts the referee Nick Katz finding a gap, Wiles's year-long attempt to repair it, and the eventual correction via insight and a companion paper; this documents the standard that major proofs must survive detailed community scrutiny and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the proof into clear structural components (deformations, cohomology, Hecke/Gorenstein properties, Selmer groups, CM cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the argument in coherent chapters/sections covering deformations of Galois representations, cohomology computations, Gorenstein/congruence properties of Hecke algebras, Selmer group estimates, and applications to elliptic curves (including ordinary CM cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiles's published paper divides the subject into numbered chapters and an appendix; a production-quality proof at this level is expected to be structured so specialists can verify each technical component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document exposition and provide accessible overviews for verification/learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the proof is complex and uses specialized jargon, provide expositions, conference proceedings, and reviews aimed at making the required topics accessible to graduate students and other researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites conference books, review articles, and shorter expositions (e.g., Faltings' bulletin, Gouvêa's article, Cornell conference notes) as necessary companion material for the community to understand, teach, and check the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue formal verification / computer-assisted checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, aim to formalize the proof in proof assistants (e.g., Lean) or otherwise enable computer verification; the article notes efforts and grants toward formalizing Wiles's proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page mentions attempts to formalize the proof and a 2024 EPSRC grant for formalisation in Lean as an indicator that machine-verifiability is a desirable long-term standard for such complex proofs.
